questions.question:
Read the below statements and select the correct option with respect to self-help groups.

(i) A self-help group is a registered group of micro-entrepreneurs.

(ii) The micro-entrepreneurs of self-help groups have similar social and economic backgrounds.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Only (ii) is true**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Self-help groups (SHGs) are typically informal groups of people who come together for a common purpose, often related to financial or social improvement.
 
• SHGs are usually composed of individuals who share similar social and economic backgrounds, facilitating mutual understanding and support.
 
• These groups are often focused on micro-entrepreneurship, where members contribute to a common fund and can take small loans from it.
 
• SHGs are not always formally registered but operate on trust and mutual benefit.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Self-Help Groups (SHGs)**

 
 
• Self-help groups are small voluntary associations of people, preferably from the same socio-economic background.
 
• They come together for the purpose of solving their common problems through self-help and mutual help.
 
• SHGs are often focused on micro-financing, where members contribute to a common fund and can take small loans from it at reasonable interest rates.
 
• They play a crucial role in the social and economic empowerment of individuals, especially women in rural areas.
 
 
 
• **Micro-entrepreneurs**
 
 
• Micro-entrepreneurs are individuals who operate very small businesses, often with minimal capital investment and few employees.
 
• These businesses are usually informal and operate on a small scale, but they provide essential goods and services to their communities.
 
• Micro-entrepreneurship is a key component of SHGs, as it allows members to improve their livelihoods through small-scale business activities.
 
 
 
• **Registration of SHGs**
 
 
• While some SHGs may choose to register formally with local authorities or organizations, many operate informally.
 
• Registration can provide SHGs with greater access to resources, government schemes, and financial services.
 
• However, the informal nature of many SHGs allows for greater flexibility and ease of operation.

questions.question: Ranjeet Singh belonged to which Misal of the Sikh community?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Sukarchakia**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Ranjeet Singh, also known as Maharaja Ranjeet Singh, was the founder of the Sikh Empire in Punjab.
 
• He belonged to the Sukarchakia Misal, one of the prominent Misals (confederacies) of the Sikh community during the 18th century.
 
• The Sukarchakia Misal was named after its founder, Nawab Sukha Singh.
 
• Ranjeet Singh successfully unified various Sikh Misals and established a powerful empire, with Lahore as its capital.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Misal**

 
 
• A Misal was a sovereign state or confederacy in the Sikh tradition, each led by a different chief or leader known as a Misaldar.
 
• There were 12 prominent Misals in the 18th-century Sikh confederacy, including Sukarchakia, Ahluwalia, Kanhaiya, and Bhangi.
 
• These Misals were primarily military and political organizations that played a crucial role in defending Sikh territories against external invasions.
 
 
 
• **Maharaja Ranjeet Singh**
 
 
• Born on 13 November 1780, Ranjeet Singh became the leader of the Sukarchakia Misal after his father's death.
 
• He is credited with establishing a unified Sikh Empire in the early 19th century, encompassing parts of present-day India and Pakistan.
 
• His reign marked the consolidation of the Sikh territories and the establishment of a strong and efficient administrative system.
 
• Ranjeet Singh's leadership and military prowess earned him the title of "Sher-e-Punjab" (Lion of Punjab).
 
 
 
• **Lahore**
 
 
• Located in present-day Pakistan, Lahore served as the capital of the Sikh Empire under Maharaja Ranjeet Singh.
 
• The city became a center of cultural, economic, and political activities during his reign.
 
• Ranjeet Singh's administration brought about significant developments in infrastructure, including the construction of roads, canals, and forts.
 
 
 
• **Sikh Empire**
 
 
• The Sikh Empire was a major power in the Indian subcontinent during the early 19th century.
 
• It was established by Maharaja Ranjeet Singh, who unified various Sikh Misals and expanded the empire's territory through conquests and alliances.
 
• The empire's administration was known for its secular policies, promoting religious tolerance and inclusivity.
 
• The Sikh Empire eventually fell to the British East India Company in the mid-19th century, following the Anglo-Sikh wars.

questions.question: In which of the following years did young leaders in Satara in Maharashtra set up a parallel government Parti Sarkar that ran People’s court and organised constructive work?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**1943**__.

__
 
• The parallel government in Satara, Maharashtra, known as Parti Sarkar, was established in **1943**.
 
• It was created by young leaders who aimed to provide an alternative governance model during the British colonial period.
 
• The Parti Sarkar ran People's courts and organized constructive work, focusing on local governance and justice.
 
• This movement was part of a broader effort to challenge British rule and demonstrate the capacity for Indian self-governance.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Parti Sarkar:**

 
 
• It was a revolutionary movement that ran a parallel government in the Satara district of Maharashtra during the British rule in India.
 
• The movement was part of the Indian freedom struggle and sought to demonstrate that Indians could govern themselves.
 
• Parti Sarkar's activities included running people's courts to settle disputes and organizing various developmental and constructive works in the region.
 
• The movement played a significant role in mobilizing local support against British colonial rule and contributed to the broader independence movement.
 
 
 
• **People's Courts:**
 
 
• These were judicial bodies set up by the Parti Sarkar to resolve disputes and administer justice outside the British legal framework.
 
• People's courts aimed to provide fair and speedy justice to the local populace, which was often denied under the British judicial system.
 
 
 
• **Constructive Work:**
 
 
• This refers to various developmental activities undertaken by the Parti Sarkar to improve the socio-economic conditions of the local people.
 
• Constructive work included initiatives in education, healthcare, agriculture, and infrastructure development.

questions.question: Ramchandra Manjhi, Padma Shri 2021 awardee, was conferred the award for which of the following contributions to art?

questions.question: Who among the following rulers strengthened the Satavahana empire in the Deccan in ancient India?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Gautamiputra Satakarni**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Gautamiputra Satakarni was one of the greatest kings of the Satavahana dynasty.
 
• He is known for his military conquests and for consolidating the Satavahana Empire in the Deccan region.
 
• He ruled from around 78 CE to 106 CE and brought significant portions of central and southern India under Satavahana control.
 
• Gautamiputra Satakarni is also credited with defeating the Saka rulers and restoring the prestige of the Satavahana dynasty.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Satavahana Dynasty**

 
 
• The Satavahana dynasty was an ancient Indian dynasty based in the Deccan region.
 
• They ruled from approximately 1st century BCE to 3rd century CE.
 
• The dynasty is known for its contributions to Indian culture, art, and architecture.
 
• The Satavahanas were also notable for their trade and maritime activities, establishing connections with the Roman Empire and other regions.
 
 
 
• **Deccan Region**
 
 
• The Deccan is a large plateau in western and southern India.
 
• It is bounded by the Western Ghats and Eastern Ghats and covers parts of modern-day Maharashtra, Telangana, Andhra Pradesh, Karnataka, and Tamil Nadu.
 
• The region has a rich history and has been ruled by various dynasties, including the Satavahanas, Chalukyas, Rashtrakutas, and others.
 
 
 
• **Saka Rulers**
 
 
• The Sakas, also known as Scythians, were a group of Iranian nomadic tribes who migrated into India around the 1st century BCE.
 
• They established several kingdoms in northwestern and western India, including the Indo-Scythian and Western Satraps kingdoms.
 
• The Saka rulers are known for their conflicts with the Satavahana dynasty and other Indian kingdoms.

• **Kuchipudi**

• It involves both dance and drama and is known for its quick footwork, dramatic expressions, and spirited movements.
 
• Kuchipudi is performed with a perfect blend of Tandava (vigorous dance) and Lasya (gentle dance).

questions.question: The Cholas as a ruling power rose to eminence in the 9th century CE when ________ seized Tanjavur from a feudatory chief of the Pallavas called Muttarayas.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Vijayalaya**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Vijayalaya Chola was the founder of the Medieval Chola dynasty.
 
• He rose to power in the 9th century CE by capturing Tanjavur from the Muttarayas, a feudatory of the Pallavas.
 
• Vijayalaya utilized the opportunity provided by the decline of the Pallavas to establish the Chola kingdom.
 
• His reign marked the beginning of the resurgence of the Chola dynasty, which later became a dominant power in South India.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Chola Dynasty**

 
 
• The Chola dynasty was one of the longest-ruling dynasties in the history of southern India.
 
• The dynasty originated in the rich Kaveri River valley.
 
• They were known for their contributions to art, architecture, and administration.
 
• The Cholas left a lasting legacy through their temples and their efficient governance, which included a highly organized administrative structure.
 
 
 
• **Tanjavur (Thanjavur)**
 
 
• It is a city in the Indian state of Tamil Nadu.
 
• Thanjavur is an important center of South Indian religion, art, and architecture.
 
• The city is home to the Brihadeshwara Temple, a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
 
• Thanjavur was the capital of the Chola dynasty during its peak.
 
 
 
• **Pallavas**
 
 
• The Pallavas were a South Indian dynasty that existed from 275 CE to 897 CE.
 
• They ruled a large portion of southern India, including the modern Tamil Nadu and Andhra Pradesh.
 
• Their capital was Kanchipuram, which was a center of learning and culture.
 
• The Pallavas were known for their architectural achievements, such as the rock-cut temples of Mahabalipuram.
 
 
 
• **Muttarayas**
 
 
• The Muttarayas were a dynasty that ruled over parts of Tamil Nadu and Karnataka.
 
• They were feudatories under the Pallavas and later became independent rulers.
 
• The Muttarayas played a significant role in the early history of the Cholas.
 
• They were known for their patronage of Jainism and Hinduism.

questions.question: Taxes levied on commodities are known as which types of taxes?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Indirect taxes**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Indirect taxes are levied on goods and services rather than on income or profits.
 
• The tax is collected by an intermediary (such as a retailer) from the person who bears the ultimate economic burden of the tax (such as the consumer).
 
• Examples of indirect taxes include Value Added Tax (VAT), Goods and Services Tax (GST), excise duty, and customs duty.
 
• Indirect taxes are typically included in the price of goods and services, making them less visible to consumers compared to direct taxes.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Corporation Taxes**

 
 
• Corporation tax is a direct tax imposed on the net income or profit of corporations and other business entities.
 
• It is calculated on the basis of the company's income and is paid directly by the company to the government.
 
 
 
• **Direct Taxes**
 
 
• Direct taxes are levied directly on the income or wealth of individuals or organizations.
 
• Examples include income tax, corporation tax, and property tax.
 
• These taxes are paid directly by the taxpayer to the government.
 
 
 
• **Indirect Taxes**
 
 
• Indirect taxes are levied on goods and services rather than on income or profits.
 
• The tax is collected by an intermediary (such as a retailer) from the person who bears the ultimate economic burden of the tax (such as the consumer).
 
• Examples include Value Added Tax (VAT), Goods and Services Tax (GST), excise duty, and customs duty.
 
• These taxes are typically included in the price of goods and services.
 
 
 
• **Both Direct and Indirect Taxes**
 
 
• Some tax systems incorporate both direct and indirect taxes to ensure a comprehensive tax structure.
 
• This combination helps in balancing the tax burden between different types of taxpayers and sectors.

questions.question: Which Article of the Constitution of India declares the Supreme Court to be a court of record?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Article 129**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Article 129 of the Constitution of India declares the Supreme Court to be a court of record.
 
• This means that the Supreme Court’s judgments, proceedings, and acts are recorded for perpetual memory and testimony.
 
• The records of the Supreme Court have evidentiary value and cannot be questioned when produced before any court.
 
• As a court of record, the Supreme Court has the power to punish for contempt of court, either with simple imprisonment or with a fine.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Article 126:**

 
 
• This article deals with the appointment of an acting Chief Justice of India.
 
• It states that when the office of Chief Justice of India is vacant or when the Chief Justice is unable to perform duties, the President can appoint an acting Chief Justice from among the judges of the Supreme Court.
 
 
 
• **Article 128:**
 
 
• This article allows for the attendance of retired judges at sittings of the Supreme Court.
 
• It states that the Chief Justice of India, with the prior consent of the President, can request any retired judge of the Supreme Court or a High Court to act as a judge of the Supreme Court for a temporary period.
 
 
 
• **Article 125:**
 
 
• This article deals with the salaries, allowances, leave of absence, pensions, etc., of the judges of the Supreme Court.
 
• It ensures that the judges receive such emoluments and privileges as determined by Parliament by law, and until so determined, as specified in the Second Schedule of the Constitution.

questions.question: Against which oppressive law did Mahatma Gandhi launch a movement in 1919 that made him a truly national leader?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Rowlatt Act**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The Rowlatt Act was passed by the British government in March 1919, which aimed at curbing the growing nationalist upsurge in India.
 
• It authorized the government to imprison any person suspected of terrorism living in British India for up to two years without a trial.
 
• This Act allowed the British to arrest and detain individuals without any judicial process and suppress press freedom.
 
• Mahatma Gandhi launched a movement against this oppressive law, leading to widespread protests and strikes, making him a national leader.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Morley-Minto Reforms**

 
 
• The Morley-Minto Reforms, also known as the Indian Councils Act 1909, introduced separate electorates for Muslims and provided for the inclusion of Indians in the governance of British India.
 
• It was an attempt to appease the demands of Indians for greater participation in the government.
 
 
 
• **Salt Tax**
 
 
• The Salt Tax was a tax levied on the production of salt, which was a basic necessity.
 
• This tax led to the famous Salt March by Mahatma Gandhi in 1930 as part of the Civil Disobedience Movement.
 
 
 
• **Vernacular Press Act**
 
 
• The Vernacular Press Act was passed in 1878 by Lord Lytton, aimed at curbing the freedom of the Indian language press.
 
• The act prohibited the publication of any material that could incite dissatisfaction or rebellion against the British government.
 
 
 
• **Rowlatt Act**
 
 
• The Rowlatt Act, officially known as the Anarchical and Revolutionary Crimes Act of 1919, gave the British government extraordinary powers to suppress subversive activities.
 
• It led to widespread unrest and was one of the precursors to the Jallianwala Bagh massacre in April 1919, where hundreds of unarmed civilians were killed.
 
• The protests against the Rowlatt Act marked a significant moment in the Indian independence movement, bringing together people from different regions and backgrounds.

• The Government of India Act of 1935 was a major legislative act passed by the British Parliament that laid the foundation for the establishment of federal structure in India.

• **Governor System:**

• **Emergency Powers:**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

• Industrial Finance Corporation of India (IFCI) is not classified as either a 'Navratna' or 'Maharatna' company in India.

• The company was established in 1948 as a statutory corporation and was later converted into a company under the Companies Act, 1956.
 
• Unlike 'Navratna' or 'Maharatna' companies, which are typically large and profitable public sector enterprises, IFCI focuses on providing financial support for industrial development.

• Navratna companies enjoy greater financial and operational autonomy compared to other PSEs.
 
• Examples of Navratna companies include Bharat Electronics Limited (BEL), Hindustan Aeronautics Limited (HAL), and National Aluminium Company Limited (NALCO).

• Maharatna companies have greater flexibility in investment and expansion decisions.

• **Industrial Finance Corporation of India (IFCI):**

• **Public Sector Enterprises (PSEs):**

• PSEs are categorized into different statuses such as Miniratna, Navratna, and Maharatna based on their performance and strategic importance.

questions.question: Which of the following state High Court's jurisdiction extends to the Union Territories of Daman and Diu?

• The Bombay High Court has jurisdiction over the state of Maharashtra and the Union Territories of Dadra and Nagar Haveli and Daman and Diu.

• **High Courts in India**

 
 
• India has a high court in each state and union territory, although some high courts have jurisdiction over more than one state or union territory.
 
• High Courts are the principal civil courts of original jurisdiction in each state and union territory, and they are empowered to hear both civil and criminal matters.
 
• They also have the power to hear appeals from lower courts and to issue writs for enforcing fundamental rights.
 
• The judges of the High Courts are appointed by the President of India in consultation with the Chief Justice of India and the governor of the state.
 
 
 
• **Union Territories of Daman and Diu**
 
 
• Daman and Diu were two separate districts of the union territory of Daman and Diu until 2019.
 
• In 2020, they were merged with Dadra and Nagar Haveli to form the new union territory of Dadra and Nagar Haveli and Daman and Diu.
 
• These territories were part of Portuguese India until they were annexed by India in 1961.
 
• The High Court with jurisdiction over these territories is the Bombay High Court.
 
 
 
• **Jurisdiction**
 
 
• Jurisdiction refers to the official power to make legal decisions and judgments.
 
• In the context of High Courts, it refers to the geographic area or the range of cases over which the court has authority.
 
• Some High Courts have jurisdiction over multiple states or union territories, while others are limited to a single state or union territory.
 
• The jurisdiction of a High Court can be extended or altered by legislation.

• Poverty is a state where an individual or community lacks the financial resources and essentials for a minimum standard of living.
 
• It is a multifaceted concept that includes social, economic, and political elements.
 
• In India, poverty is often measured using income levels and consumption patterns.
 
 
 
• **Poverty Line in India**
 
 
• The poverty line is an economic benchmark used to measure the minimum level of income required to secure the necessities of life.
 
• In India, the poverty line is determined by the Planning Commission based on the expenditure required for a minimum calorific intake and other basic needs.
 
• As per the Tendulkar Committee report, the poverty line is based on consumption expenditure and includes spending on food, education, health, etc.
 
 
 
• **2011 Census**
 
 
• The Census of India 2011 was the 15th National Census since 1871 and was conducted by the Census Commissioner of India.
 
• The census collected data on various socio-economic parameters including population, poverty levels, literacy rates, housing conditions, and employment.

questions.question: Terrace farming is commonly practiced in which of the following regions of India?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Himalayan region**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Terrace farming is a traditional agricultural practice in the **Himalayan region** due to its steep slopes and mountainous terrain.
 
• It helps in reducing soil erosion and water runoff, which are common issues in hilly areas.
 
• Terrace farming allows for the cultivation of various crops such as rice, maize, and potatoes, which are essential for the local populations.
 
• This method of farming is crucial for maximizing arable land area and ensuring food security in the Himalayan region.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Terrace Farming**

 
 
• Terrace farming is a method of carving steps or terraces into the slopes of hilly or mountainous regions to create flat areas for agriculture.
 
• This technique helps in retaining soil moisture, preventing soil erosion, and making efficient use of water.
 
• It is commonly used in areas with uneven terrain where traditional farming methods are not feasible.
 
 
 
• **Himalayan Region**
 
 
• The Himalayas are a mountain range in South Asia, separating the plains of the Indian subcontinent from the Tibetan Plateau.
 
• The region is known for its high peaks, including Mount Everest, the highest point on Earth.
 
• The climate and topography of the Himalayas make terrace farming an essential practice for local agriculture.
 
 
 
• **Soil Erosion**
 
 
• Soil erosion is the process by which the top layer of soil is removed by natural forces such as wind and water.
 
• It is a significant issue in hilly areas where heavy rainfall and steep slopes can lead to rapid loss of fertile soil.
 
• Terrace farming helps to mitigate soil erosion by creating flat surfaces that reduce the speed of water runoff.
 
 
 
• **Water Runoff**
 
 
• Water runoff refers to the flow of water, typically from precipitation, over the surface of the land.
 
• In hilly regions, rapid water runoff can lead to soil erosion and loss of nutrients from the soil.
 
• Terracing helps to slow down water runoff and allows for better absorption of water by the soil.

• **Scoring in Archery**
 
 
• Each arrow shot scores points based on where it lands on the target.

• The total score for an end is the sum of the points from all arrows shot in that end.
 
 
 
• **Time Management**

• Archers often practice shooting within the time limit to develop a consistent rhythm and avoid time-related penalties.

• **Protein Content in Plants**

• They are widely distributed across the globe, found in temperate and tropical regions.
 
• Wolffia thrives in nutrient-rich waters and can form dense mats on the surface of water bodies.

questions.question: What is the common biological phenomenon by which one organism produces biochemicals that influence the growth, survival, development, and reproduction of other organisms known as?

__
 
• **Allelopathy** refers to the biological phenomenon by which one organism produces biochemicals that influence the growth, survival, development, and reproduction of other organisms.
 
• The biochemicals involved are called **allelochemicals** and can have beneficial or detrimental effects on target organisms.
 
• Allelopathy is commonly observed in plants, where certain plants release chemicals that can inhibit the germination or growth of neighboring plants.
 
• This phenomenon plays a significant role in **agriculture, horticulture, and forestry**, as it can affect crop yields and plant biodiversity.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Allotropy**

 
 
• Allotropy refers to the existence of two or more different forms of an element in the same physical state.
 
• Examples include carbon, which can exist as diamond, graphite, and graphene.
 
• Allotropic forms have different physical properties and chemical behaviors.
 
 
 
• **Allopathy**
 
 
• Allopathy is a term used to describe the mainstream medical use of pharmacologically active agents or physical interventions to treat or suppress symptoms or pathophysiologic processes of diseases or conditions.
 
• It is often contrasted with homeopathy, a different system of medicine.
 
 
 
• **Allelomorph**
 
 
• Allelomorph, now commonly referred to as an allele, is one of two or more versions of a gene that are found at the same place on a chromosome.
 
• Alleles can result in different traits, such as eye color or blood type.
 
• The combination of alleles that an individual has is known as their genotype.

• They are non-justiciable in nature, meaning they are not enforceable by any court but are considered fundamental in the governance of the country.

questions.question: Which of the following Articles of the Indian Constitution deals with fundamental duties?

__
 
• **Article 51A** of the Indian Constitution enumerates the Fundamental Duties of every citizen of India.
 
• These duties were added by the **42nd Amendment Act** in 1976, upon the recommendations of the Swaran Singh Committee.
 
• Originally, there were 10 Fundamental Duties, but the **86th Amendment Act** of 2002 added an 11th duty.
 
• The Fundamental Duties are non-justiciable, meaning they are not legally enforceable by the courts for their violation.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **42nd Amendment Act (1976)**

 
 
• The 42nd Amendment Act is also known as the "Mini-Constitution" because of its wide-ranging changes to the Constitution of India.
 
• This amendment added the Fundamental Duties to the Constitution in response to the internal and external challenges faced by the country.
 
• It aimed to balance citizens' rights with their duties to ensure that rights are enjoyed responsibly.
 
 
 
• **Swaran Singh Committee**
 
 
• The Swaran Singh Committee was appointed by the Government of India to make recommendations on the constitutional amendments to be made.
 
• The committee recommended the inclusion of Fundamental Duties in the Indian Constitution.
 
• It was named after Dr. Swaran Singh, who was the then Union Minister of External Affairs.
 
 
 
• **86th Amendment Act (2002)**
 
 
• The 86th Amendment Act added the 11th Fundamental Duty which states: "A parent or guardian must provide opportunities for education to their child or ward between the ages of six and fourteen."
 
• This amendment also made education a fundamental right for children in this age group under Article 21A.
 
 
 
• **Non-justiciable Nature of Fundamental Duties**
 
 
• Unlike Fundamental Rights, Fundamental Duties are non-justiciable, meaning they cannot be enforced by law through judicial means.
 
• However, they act as a moral obligation for citizens and aim to promote a sense of discipline and commitment towards the nation.

questions.question: Which of the following is the most reactive metal?

__
 
• Magnesium is a highly reactive metal, especially when compared to other metals like lead, zinc, and mercury.
 
• It belongs to the alkali earth metal group and has the atomic number 12.
 
• It reacts readily with water to form magnesium hydroxide and hydrogen gas, and it also reacts vigorously with acids and other substances.
 
• Due to its high reactivity, magnesium is often used in pyrotechnics, flares, and incendiary devices.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Reactivity of Metals:**

 
 
• Reactivity of metals refers to how easily they undergo chemical reactions, especially with acids, water, and oxygen.
 
• Highly reactive metals can lose their electrons easily and form positive ions.
 
• Reactivity series is a list of metals arranged in order of their reactivity from highest to lowest.
 
 
 
• **Alkali Earth Metals:**
 
 
• The alkali earth metals are a group of elements in the second group of the periodic table.
 
• They include beryllium, magnesium, calcium, strontium, barium, and radium.
 
• These metals are known for their high reactivity and are usually found in compound form in nature.
 
 
 
• **Uses of Magnesium:**
 
 
• Magnesium is used in the manufacturing of lightweight materials for cars and airplanes.
 
• It is also used in the production of electronics, such as laptops and mobile phones, due to its strength and low density.
 
• In the health industry, magnesium compounds are used as dietary supplements and in medicines to treat magnesium deficiency.
 
 
 
• **Safety Precautions with Magnesium:**
 
 
• Due to its high reactivity, magnesium should be handled with care, especially in powdered form.
 
• It should be stored in a cool, dry place away from moisture and sources of ignition.
 
• When burning, magnesium produces a very bright white light and can cause severe eye damage; hence, proper eye protection should be worn.

questions.question: From which country is the power of judicial review taken in the Indian Constitution?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**United States of America**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The concept of judicial review in the Indian Constitution is derived from the Constitution of the **United States of America (USA).**
 
• Judicial review refers to the power of the judiciary to interpret the constitutionality of laws and executive actions.
 
• In the USA, the concept was established in the landmark case of **Marbury v. Madison** (1803).
 
• It ensures that the laws passed by the legislature and actions taken by the executive are in accordance with the Constitution.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Judicial Review**

 
 
• It is a process under which executive or legislative actions are subject to review by the judiciary.
 
• It is an essential function of the judiciary to safeguard the supremacy of the Constitution and to protect the fundamental rights of citizens.
 
• In India, judicial review is considered a basic feature of the Constitution, which cannot be amended or taken away by the Parliament.
 
• Articles 32 and 226 of the Indian Constitution provide the basis for judicial review of legislative and executive actions.
 
 
 
• **Marbury v. Madison (1803)**
 
 
• This case is significant in American constitutional history as it established the principle of judicial review in the United States.
 
• The case was decided by the Supreme Court under Chief Justice John Marshall.
 
• The ruling declared that the Supreme Court had the power to nullify an act of Congress if it was found to be in conflict with the Constitution.
 
 
 
• **Indian Constitution and Judicial Review**
 
 
• The Indian Constitution explicitly confers the power of judicial review on the judiciary through Articles 13, 32, 131-136, 143, 226, and 246.
 
• The Constitution of India provides a system of checks and balances to ensure that no organ of the government exceeds its powers.
 
• Judicial review in India plays a critical role in maintaining the rule of law and ensuring the protection of fundamental rights.

questions.question: In which Indian state is the cave site of Bagh located?

questions.question: Surya Sen was associated with which of the following radical activities against British?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Chittagong Armory Raid**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Surya Sen, popularly known as Master Da, was a prominent Indian freedom fighter and the chief architect of the Chittagong Armory Raid.
 
• The Chittagong Armory Raid took place on 18 April 1930 in Chittagong, then part of British India (now in Bangladesh).
 
• Surya Sen led a group of revolutionaries in an attempt to raid the British armory in Chittagong and seize weapons to fight against the British rule.
 
• The raid was an important event in the history of Indian independence movement as it demonstrated the spirit and determination of Indian revolutionaries.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Kakori Conspiracy**

 
 
• The Kakori Conspiracy was an armed robbery on the Kakori train near Lucknow on 9 August 1925 by the Hindustan Republican Association (HRA).
 
• Prominent revolutionaries involved included Ram Prasad Bismil, Ashfaqulla Khan, and Chandrashekhar Azad.
 
• The objective was to fund their revolutionary activities by looting the government treasury carried in the train.
 
 
 
• **Muzaffarpur Conspiracy Case**
 
 
• This was an assassination attempt on the British official Kingsford by Indian revolutionaries Khudiram Bose and Prafulla Chaki on 30 April 1908.
 
• The attack took place in Muzaffarpur, Bihar, but resulted in the death of two British women instead of Kingsford.
 
• Khudiram Bose was later arrested and executed, becoming a martyr in the Indian independence movement.
 
 
 
• **Delhi Conspiracy Case**
 
 
• This was a plot to assassinate the then Viceroy of India, Lord Hardinge, during a procession in Delhi on 23 December 1912.
 
• The attack was planned by Rash Behari Bose and Basanta Kumar Biswas, who threw a bomb at Lord Hardinge's elephant.
 
• Although Lord Hardinge was injured, he survived the attack.
 
 
 
• **Chittagong Armory Raid**
 
 
• The raid was an attempt by Indian revolutionaries to raid the armory of the police and auxiliary forces from the Chittagong armory on 18 April 1930.
 
• Surya Sen led a group of revolutionaries in this endeavor, with the aim of destroying the British control over the region.
 
• Although they were unable to achieve their ultimate goal, the raid inspired many and highlighted the bravery and commitment of the revolutionaries.
 
• Surya Sen was eventually captured and hanged by the British on 12 January 1934.

questions.question: As per the Indus Water Treaty 1960, how much per cent water can India use from the river?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**20 per cent**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The Indus Water Treaty (IWT) was signed between India and Pakistan on 19th September 1960, with the World Bank being a signatory as well.
 
• Under the treaty, India was allocated the unrestricted use of all the waters of the eastern rivers (Sutlej, Beas, and Ravi) while Pakistan was allocated the western rivers (Indus, Jhelum, and Chenab).
 
• India, however, is entitled to use 20% of the total water carried by the Indus river system for irrigation, power generation, and transport purposes.
 
• The treaty has been a successful example of conflict resolution between two countries sharing water resources.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Indus Water Treaty (IWT)**

 
 
• The IWT is a water-distribution treaty between India and Pakistan, brokered by the World Bank. It was signed in Karachi on 19 September 1960 by then Prime Minister of India Jawaharlal Nehru and then President of Pakistan Ayub Khan.
 
• The treaty allocates the use of the river waters of the Indus basin between India and Pakistan. The basin comprises six rivers: the Indus, Jhelum, Chenab, Ravi, Beas, and Sutlej.
 
• The treaty gives India control over the waters of the three eastern rivers – the Beas, the Ravi, and the Sutlej, while Pakistan has control over the waters of the three western rivers – the Indus, the Jhelum, and the Chenab.
 
• The treaty allows India to use the water of the western rivers for limited irrigation use and unrestricted use for power generation, domestic use, and non-consumptive use like navigation, fish culture, etc.
 
 
 
• **Water Sharing**
 
 
• India is allowed to use 20% of the water from the western rivers for purposes such as irrigation, power generation, and transport. This amounts to around 3.6 million acre-feet (MAF) of water.
 
• The treaty specifies that the flow of the rivers shall not be obstructed by any party, ensuring a continuous supply of water to both countries.
 
 
 
• **Conflict Resolution**
 
 
• The IWT has a permanent Indus Commission with a commissioner from each country, which meets regularly to discuss and resolve any issues that arise.
 
• In case of disputes, the treaty outlines a process of arbitration which involves a neutral expert appointed by the World Bank.

questions.question: Which dynasty ruled after the Tuglaq dynasty?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Sayyid dynasty**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The Sayyid dynasty was founded by Khizr Khan who claimed to be a descendant of Prophet Muhammad.
 
• It ruled the Delhi Sultanate from 1414 to 1451.
 
• The Sayyid dynasty succeeded the Tughlaq dynasty and preceded the Lodi dynasty.
 
• During the Sayyid rule, the Delhi Sultanate faced numerous internal and external challenges, including invasions and internal revolts.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Tughlaq dynasty**

 
 
• The Tughlaq dynasty ruled the Delhi Sultanate from 1320 to 1413.
 
• Founded by Ghiyath al-Din Tughlaq, it is known for its administrative reforms and architectural achievements, including the fort of Tughlaqabad in Delhi.
 
• The most notable ruler was Muhammad bin Tughlaq, known for his ambitious but often impractical policies, including the transfer of the capital from Delhi to Daulatabad.
 
• Despite its initial success, the dynasty faced severe challenges, including revolts and invasions, leading to its eventual decline.
 
 
 
• **Lodi dynasty**
 
 
• The Lodi dynasty was the last dynasty of the Delhi Sultanate, ruling from 1451 to 1526.
 
• Founded by Bahlul Lodi, it was a Pashtun dynasty and marked the beginning of Afghan rule in India.
 
• The most notable ruler was Sikandar Lodi, who expanded the territory and improved administrative efficiency.
 
• The dynasty ended with the defeat of Ibrahim Lodi by Babur in the Battle of Panipat in 1526, leading to the establishment of the Mughal Empire.
 
 
 
• **Khalji dynasty**
 
 
• The Khalji dynasty ruled the Delhi Sultanate from 1290 to 1320.
 
• Founded by Jalal-ud-din Khalji, it is known for its military campaigns and expansion of the Sultanate's territory.
 
• Alauddin Khalji, the most prominent ruler, implemented significant economic and administrative reforms and successfully defended the Sultanate against Mongol invasions.
 
• The dynasty came to an end with the assassination of the last Khalji ruler, Qutb-ud-din Mubarak Shah, by his own nobles.
 
 
 
• **Mamluk dynasty**
 
 
• The Mamluk dynasty, also known as the Slave dynasty, ruled the Delhi Sultanate from 1206 to 1290.
 
• It was founded by Qutb-ud-din Aibak, a former slave of Muhammad of Ghor, who became the first Sultan of Delhi.
 
• The dynasty is known for its architectural contributions, including the construction of the Qutb Minar.
 
• The Mamluk dynasty ended with the rise of the Khalji dynasty in 1290.

questions.question: In Olympic archery events, how many concentric rings are there which represent different scoring sectors?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**10**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• In Olympic archery events, there are **10 concentric rings** on the target.
 
• Each ring represents a different scoring sector, with scores ranging from 1 to 10.
 
• The innermost ring, known as the "bullseye," scores the highest points, which is **10 points**.
 
• The target face used in Olympic archery has a diameter of 122 cm, and the rings are arranged concentrically.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Target Face:**

 
 
• The target face in Olympic archery is a circular sheet of paper or synthetic material.
 
• The diameter of the target face is 122 cm for recurve archery and 80 cm for compound archery.
 
 
 
• **Scoring Zones:**
 
 
• The target is divided into 10 concentric scoring zones, with each zone having a different point value from 1 to 10.
 
• The outermost ring scores 1 point, and the scores increase by 1 point for each inner ring, culminating in the bullseye which scores 10 points.
 
 
 
• **Bullseye:**
 
 
• The bullseye is the center-most ring of the target and scores 10 points.
 
• It is also sometimes referred to as the "gold" due to its color.

questions.question: Which elements act as hygroscopic nuclei around which water vapour condenses to produce clouds?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Dust and sea salt**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Hygroscopic nuclei are tiny particles that attract water molecules from the air.
 
• Dust and sea salt serve as primary hygroscopic nuclei in the atmosphere.
 
• These particles facilitate the condensation of water vapor into liquid droplets, forming clouds.
 
• Without hygroscopic nuclei, the formation of clouds would be significantly less efficient.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Hygroscopic Nuclei:**

 
 
• These are tiny particles suspended in the atmosphere that have the ability to attract and hold water molecules.
 
• Examples include dust, sea salt, smoke, and certain types of pollution.
 
• They are crucial for the process of cloud formation as they provide surfaces for water vapor to condense upon.
 
• Hygroscopic nuclei are essential for the formation of raindrops, which eventually fall to the ground as precipitation.
 
 
 
• **Condensation:**
 
 
• Condensation is the process by which water vapor in the air is changed into liquid water.
 
• This process is essential for cloud formation and occurs when air is cooled to its dew point or when it becomes saturated with water vapor.
 
• Condensation releases latent heat, which can affect atmospheric stability and weather patterns.
 
 
 
• **Cloud Formation:**
 
 
• Clouds form when moist air rises and cools, causing the water vapor to condense onto hygroscopic nuclei.
 
• The types of clouds that form depend on various factors, including the altitude at which condensation occurs and the atmospheric conditions.
 
• Clouds are categorized into different types such as cumulus, stratus, cirrus, and nimbus based on their appearance and altitude.
 
 
 
• **Sea Salt:**
 
 
• Sea salt particles are created from the evaporation of seawater and are a major component of atmospheric aerosols.
 
• These particles are highly effective at attracting water molecules, making them excellent hygroscopic nuclei.
 
• Sea salt particles contribute significantly to cloud formation, especially in coastal and marine environments.

questions.question: The first electric train ran in which state of India in the year 1925?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Maharashtra**__.

• Railway electrification involves converting conventional railway tracks and systems to be powered by electricity.
 
• This process includes the installation of overhead wires, substations, and other infrastructure to support electric locomotives and trains.
 
• Electric trains are generally more efficient, environmentally friendly, and cost-effective compared to diesel-powered trains.
 
• Globally, many countries have undertaken extensive railway electrification projects to modernize their rail networks.
 
 
 
• **Great Indian Peninsula Railway (GIPR):**
 
 
• The Great Indian Peninsula Railway was one of the pioneering railway companies in India.
 
• It was established in 1849 and played a significant role in the development of the Indian railway network.
 
• The GIPR operated in the western and central parts of India, primarily in Maharashtra and surrounding regions.
 
• It was later merged into the Indian Railways network, which is now one of the largest railway systems in the world.
 
 
 
• **History of Indian Railways:**
 
 
• Indian Railways is the fourth-largest railway network in the world by size.
 
• The first passenger train in India ran on April 16, 1853, between Bombay (Mumbai) and Thane.
 
• Indian Railways has played a crucial role in the economic and social development of the country.
 
• It continues to be a vital mode of transportation for millions of passengers and tonnes of freight across India.

questions.question: Initially, which of the following was the capital of Magadha Mahajanapada?

__
 
• Rajagaha, also known as Rajgir, was the initial capital of the Magadha Mahajanapada, an important kingdom in ancient India.
 
• It was one of the major cities during the time of Gautama Buddha and was a prominent center of political and spiritual activities.
 
• Rajagaha is known for its strategic location, surrounded by five hills, which made it a well-protected and fortified city.
 
• It later became an important site for both Jainism and Buddhism, with numerous monasteries and historical sites related to these religions.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Magadha Mahajanapada:**

 
 
• Magadha was one of the sixteen Mahajanapadas (great kingdoms) of ancient India, located in present-day Bihar.
 
• It played a significant role in the history of India, being the center of the Maurya and Gupta empires, which significantly contributed to Indian civilization.
 
• The region was known for its rich culture, economic prosperity, and strategic military importance.
 
 
 
• **Pataliputra:**
 
 
• Pataliputra later became the capital of Magadha after Rajagaha. It was founded by Ajatashatru, the king of Magadha, and became a major political and cultural hub.
 
• Pataliputra was the capital city during the reign of the Maurya dynasty, including Emperor Ashoka, and continued to be an important city during the Gupta period.
 
 
 
• **Vaishali:**
 
 
• Vaishali was another significant ancient city, known for being the capital of the Licchavi republic and an important center for both Buddhism and Jainism.
 
• It is notable for its association with Lord Mahavira and Gautama Buddha, who spent considerable time here.
